messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Liam is a 21-year-old white American man who came to treatment several months after a violent injury to a close family member, an event he still cannot tell in a smooth, ordinary way. When he tries, his speech stalls and fragments. He circles around it, then goes quiet, as if the experience exists in hard snapshots rather than a story. What comes most clearly are images: a particular part of his loved one’s body after the injury, fixed in his mind with a cruel sharpness, “like photographs,” and the smell that was in the air at the time, which returns so vividly that for a moment he feels he is back there again rather than remembering from a distance.

Since then, Liam has lived with a sense that danger can break through at any moment. If someone nearby moves suddenly, he is on guard before he has time to think. In those moments his body reacts fast and completely, and he has come to believe with bitterness that his body is no longer on his side. Even when he knows where he is, even when his wife tells him he is safe, his heart and muscles respond as if the emergency is still unfolding. What frightens him is not only the reaction itself but what it seems to say about him. He has begun to think he cannot rely on himself anymore, that some basic steadiness is gone.

The triggers in daily life are painfully specific. Seeing body parts associated with the injury can stop him cold; he finds his attention locking onto them before he can look away. Comments about family can do the same, especially casual remarks that would once have passed without notice. He hears them as loaded now, as if they could open the whole scene again. People who seem suspicious to him—someone watching too closely, lingering, moving unpredictably—make him tense immediately. Because he is unemployed, he spends much of his time in ordinary public and domestic settings where these moments catch him off guard: a stranger shifting abruptly in a checkout line, a neighbor making an offhand family comment, a scene in a waiting room where his eyes land on the wrong physical detail. The world feels full of traps he cannot reliably anticipate.

At times the past does not feel past. He describes sudden episodes in which it is as though the event is happening again. He may freeze, stare, or react to what is in his mind rather than what is around him. Afterwards he is shaken and ashamed. The smell from the original event can return during these episodes, which makes them feel even more real. At night he struggles to fall asleep and often cannot stay asleep. The dark and quiet do not bring rest; instead they leave him alone with the possibility of being pulled back into those images. Over time he has become wary of being alone in a room or building at all. He waits for his wife to come home, follows her from room to room, or keeps himself near other people because solitude feels too exposed.

He has also narrowed his life in quieter ways. He avoids television programs, films, and news stories that might resemble what happened. What used to be casual background entertainment now feels dangerous, as if one unexpected scene could overwhelm him. These habits have made his days smaller. Being unemployed has left him without the routines that once helped define him, and he now speaks as if that version of himself has been lost. He says he is no longer capable of doing the things that defined him, though he says this less as a dramatic statement than as a conclusion he has drawn from repeated moments of freezing, panicking, and withdrawing.

When the feelings crest and he cannot settle them, Liam sometimes hurts himself physically to release the pressure. He describes it as a way to cut through the unbearable build-up in his body when he feels overwhelmed. He does not present this as wanting to die, but as a desperate attempt to get temporary control over sensations that otherwise seem to own him.

His marriage has become both a comfort and a strain. His wife has seen how rarely he can be by himself now, how quickly a stranger’s sudden movement can change his whole demeanor, how a remark about family can make him go silent and distant. What finally brought him in was the growing sense that his world was shrinking around these reactions and that he was becoming someone he did not recognize. He wants help making sense of what happened, especially because he still feels unable to put it into words. Most of all, he is afraid that this is permanent—that he will remain watchful, unreliable to himself, and unable to return to the life he thought was his.
